t: From the 1st millennium BCE to the Spanish conquest, the Maya of southern Mexico and Central America built hundreds of cities, from El Mirador and Tikal to Chichén Itzá, but never a single state.
Their scribes created the most complete writing system of the ancient Americas, recording the deeds of holy kings in precisely dated inscriptions, most of which have been deciphered since the 1950s.
The southern lowland cities were abandoned in the 9th and 10th centuries, but Maya kingdoms lasted in Yucatán and the highlands until the Spanish conquest, and well over six million Maya live today.
dyk: In 2018 an airborne laser survey of the forests of northern Guatemala revealed more than 60,000 ancient Maya structures, from houses and reservoirs to causeways and defensive walls, many of them previously unknown.
ev: Maya farming communities build the first great ceremonial platforms, at Ceibal and Aguada Fénix
El Mirador flourishes, its La Danta complex rising some 70 metres above the forest floor
Siyaj K’ak', a war leader linked with Teotihuacan, arrives at Tikal and a new dynasty takes power
K’inich Janaab Pakal begins his 68-year reign at Palenque
In the Classic Maya collapse the southern lowland kingdoms stop raising monuments, and their cities empty
Chichén Itzá is the leading power of northern Yucatán
Pedro de Alvarado conquers the K’iche' kingdom of the Guatemalan highlands
The Spanish take Nojpetén, capital of the Itza, the last independent Maya kingdom

f.homeland: The Yucatán Peninsula and the lands to its south: south-eastern Mexico (Chiapas, Tabasco, Campeche, Yucatán and Quintana Roo), Guatemala, Belize and the western parts of Honduras and El Salvador
f.period: c. 2000 BCE–1697 CE: the Preclassic period until c. 250 CE, the Classic c. 250–900, and the Postclassic until the Spanish conquest, completed with the fall of Nojpetén in 1697
f.known: Hieroglyphic writing, the Long Count calendar and astronomy; temple-pyramids and palaces at Tikal, Palenque, Copán and Chichén Itzá; rival dynasties of holy kings; the Classic Maya collapse
f.sources: The ruined cities and their inscriptions, most of which can now be read; four surviving pre-conquest books; Spanish accounts such as that of Diego de Landa; colonial writings in Maya languages, such as the Popol Vuh and the Books of Chilam Balam; the living Maya peoples
